newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Trade envoys fight over key policy declaration.
newsitem.headline: Trade envoys fight over key policy declaration.

text.p: Envoys to the World Trade Organisation battled on Friday over the text of a key declaration on the global trade agenda into the 21st century.

Argument centred on a draft of the document to be issued at a WTO trade conference next month which contains references to the contentious issues of linking labour standards and trade, as well as investment and competition policies.
The five-day conference opening in Singapore on December 9 will be the first to bring together trade ministers and delegates from the WTO's 125 member countries.
"There is little sign of compromise at the moment," said one trade diplomat as an informal meeting to try to finalise a text got under way.
The declaration proposed by WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero was due to have been completed two weeks ago.

Major developing countries have said they cannot accept the so-called "new issues". They argue that the bid to include them in a WTO work programme for the next few years is part of a Western effort to sap their national economic strength.

But the United States is pushing very hard for formal acceptance that the labour issue must be handled within the WTO. The European Union wants an accord on competition policy. Japan and Canada, backed by the EU, seek a deal on investment.
Trade envoys say, however, that agreement on a final text before Singapore now looks highly unlikely, and it could be left to the ministers themselves to finesse a document that all can accept.

The text submitted on Friday by Ruggiero, a former Italian trade minister who has campaigned for better treatment of the world's poorest countries by the big trading powers, clearly sought to strike a balance between bitterly opposing views on the labour issue.

It proposes that the ministers declare they "renew our commitment to the observance of core labour standards and our support for the work of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) in promoting these standards".

Emerging economies, who see the bid to link labour standards with trade through enforceable WTO rules as aimed at hitting the advantage they have from lower labour costs, also want to keep the issue in the United Nations agency.

The Ruggiero draft would also have the ministers say that "the contribution the WTO can make to the promotion of such standards is through increased adherence to the rule-based system, together with further trade liberalisation and the economic growth fostered by increased trade."
"We agree that protectionist measures should not be used to enforce labour standards, and that the competitive advantage of low-wage countries should not be put into question," it adds.

Trade analysts said this formulation was unlikely to go far enough to satisfy the United States -- or international trade union organisations who will be sending their leaders to Singapore -- and could also displease developing countries.

In a phrasing that emerging economies are also resisting, the text would have the ministers agree to "begin an examination of the relationship between trade and investment" with an eventual report to the WTO's ruling General Council.

It also would commit ministers to setting up an experts' group to study the relationship between competition policy and the WTO and "identify any problems that may require action in the WTO framework".
Emerging economies fear that any discussion, once begun, would lead to formulation of rules that would prevent them following policies aimed at national industrial development.
